opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest shift for me was realizing that "the brain" isn't one thing. When we started, the mental model was pretty clean: you have a big model that sees the world, understands the language instruction, and outputs actions. Vision, language, action, one pipeline. On paper that looks like a brain.

But once you actually try to put it on a real robot, in a real environment, you discover that a lot of what matters isn't the high-level decision at all. It's everything underneath. The model might correctly understand "pick up the cup and put it in the sink," and it might even pick a reasonable trajectory, but then the gripper hits the cup at a slightly wrong angle, the cup slides, and the whole thing falls apart. The semantic part was right; the physical part wasn't. In the lab you can hide that with curated scenes. In deployment you can't.

So the first lesson was about timescales. Language-level reasoning can happen at a fairly slow rate, a few times a second is fine. But contact, force, balance, those loops need to run much faster, and they need to react to feedback the big model never sees in time. If you try to make one giant model handle everything at one frequency, you either get something too slow to be stable, or something that's fast but doesn't really understand what it's doing. That pushed us toward thinking in layers, something closer to a slow "thinking" system and a fast "reflex" system, with a clear interface between them.

The second lesson was about what "action" even means. Early on we treated actions like another token stream, like text. But actions are grounded in a specific body. The same instruction maps to very different motor commands on a different arm, a different hand, a different camera placement. So the brain doesn't just need to control joints; it needs a representation of the body it's in, and some way to transfer across bodies. That's where a lot of the real difficulty lives.

And the third thing, which is maybe more philosophical, is that a robot brain has to control its own uncertainty. A chatbot can be confidently wrong and you just regenerate. A robot that's confidently wrong breaks something. So knowing when it doesn't know, slowing down, re-observing, asking, retrying, that turns out to be part of control too, not an afterthought.

So I'd summarize it this way: before deployment, I thought the brain needed to control the robot. After deployment, I think the brain needs to control the relationship between understanding and the physical world: timing, embodiment, and doubt. The understanding part, frankly, is the part that's progressing fastest. The rest is where the hard engineering is.

fable-5.1.text:
When we started trying to actually deploy a Vision-Language-Action model, the first thing that fell apart was my assumption that the "brain" was the whole story. In the lab, you treat the model as the system. You give it an image and an instruction, it emits an action, and the benchmark goes up. But the moment it sits on a real arm in a real room, you realize the model is sitting on top of this enormous stack of things it has no idea exist. Latency in the camera pipeline. Calibration drift between the wrist camera and the gripper. A controller that interpolates between waypoints in a way the training data never captured. The model was trained on the output of that stack, not on the stack itself.

So the first shift was about the action space. We had been thinking of actions as something like the poses in the dataset, end-effector deltas at some fixed frequency. On hardware you discover that what you really need to control is a layered thing. There's a high-level intent, maybe where the hand should go in the next half second. Below that there's a question of how fast, with how much force, how compliant the arm should be when it hits something unexpectedly. Humans do this without thinking. A VLA trained purely on positional trajectories has no concept of force at all, so it just pushes until the controller saturates. We spent a lot of time asking whether the model should output force, or impedance parameters, or whether that belongs to a lower layer the model never sees. I don't think the field has settled that. My current view is that the model should predict something closer to a short horizon of desired behavior, and a fast local controller should own the physics.

The second shift was about time. A seven billion parameter model running at a few hertz is fine for deciding what to do, and terrible for deciding how to do it this instant. When you deploy, you feel that gap immediately. The arm moves, the world changes, and the model is still thinking about the frame from three hundred milliseconds ago. So you end up with action chunking, with asynchronous inference, with the model emitting a little plan that something faster executes. That design comes out of deployment pain, not from theory. It also made me realize the brain's job is partly to predict what the world will look like when its own command actually lands.

The third thing, and maybe the most humbling, was the failure modes. In simulation the model fails by doing something wrong. On real hardware it fails by doing something slightly wrong, repeatedly, and the errors compound. A gripper closes two millimeters early, the object rotates, now the scene is out of distribution, and the model has no mechanism to notice it's drifting. That told me the brain needs some sense of its own uncertainty, or at least a way to detect "this doesn't look like anything I've seen" and slow down or re-grasp. Pure imitation doesn't give you that. You get confident nonsense.

And the last piece is the data loop. Deployment taught me that the model you ship is really just the first version of a data collection instrument. The interesting signal isn't the demonstrations you started with, it's the places where the robot got stuck in someone's kitchen. If your system can't capture those moments, correct them, and feed them back, the brain stays frozen at whatever the lab looked like. So I came away thinking a robot brain isn't one network. It's a slow thinking layer, a fast control layer, a reflex that knows when to be scared, and a pipeline that lets all of that learn from being wrong in the real world.

astra-6.text:
Trying to deploy VRA made me think of the robot brain less as something that produces an action and more as something that has to keep an entire interaction working. Choosing the right action is only one part. You also have to execute it at the right time, observe what actually happened, and adjust when the result differs from what you expected.

For example, “pick up the object” sounds like one decision. But the robot has to approach it, establish contact, close the gripper, and determine whether the grasp succeeded. If it misses, the next step shouldn’t simply continue the original plan.

So the shift for me was from predicting actions to controlling a continuous feedback loop. The brain needs to connect the task-level intention with the physical execution, including knowing when to continue, when to stop, and when to try something else.

sol-6.1.text:
Trying to deploy VRA made me think beyond the model’s next prediction and focus on the whole control loop. A robot’s action changes the world, and that changes what it sees next. So the brain needs to keep observing, recognize when an action hasn’t worked, and adjust.

That also changes what you mean by control. It’s not just deciding where the arm should move. It’s deciding when to move, how to coordinate with the rest of the body, and when to stop or try again. The high-level intention has to connect to reliable physical execution. A good prediction is useful, but the real test is whether the robot can keep making progress when things don’t go exactly as expected.
